lead: A mixer is a three-port circuit that multiplies two signals. The radio-frequency (RF) port carries the signal, the local-oscillator (LO) port carries a strong sine or square wave, and the intermediate-frequency (IF) port carries the product. Multiplication creates sum and difference frequencies, so a mixer moves a signal from one band to another without changing its modulation: down to an IF or baseband in a receiver, up to the radio band in a transmitter. Its conversion gain, noise figure, port isolation, linearity and spurious responses decide how clean that translation is.
prereq: You need: the image frequency from receiver architectures and IIP3 from nonlinearity.

blocks.text: Multiplying A cos ω<sub>RF</sub>t by cos ω<sub>LO</sub>t gives (A/2)[cos(ω<sub>LO</sub> − ω<sub>RF</sub>)t + cos(ω<sub>LO</sub> + ω<sub>RF</sub>)t]: half the amplitude at the difference and half at the sum. A filter after the mixer keeps the one that is wanted.

items: Down-conversion (receiver): the RF and LO inputs give f<sub>IF</sub> = |f<sub>RF</sub> − f<sub>LO</sub>|; a filter keeps the difference.
Up-conversion (transmitter): the IF and LO inputs give f<sub>LO</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub> and f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>IF</sub>; a filter keeps one, the other is the unwanted sideband.
Either way the image, the second input that gives the same output (2f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>RF</sub>), must be removed before the mixer or cancelled by an image-reject mixer.

blocks.text: Real mixers switch rather than multiply: the LO turns diodes or transistors fully on and off, which is the same as multiplying by a square wave. A square wave contains the odd harmonics 3f<sub>LO</sub>, 5f<sub>LO</sub> and so on, and any nonlinearity adds powers of the RF signal. So the output contains every product |m·f<sub>LO</sub> ± n·f<sub>RF</sub>| for whole numbers m and n. A spur, or spurious response, is any input frequency other than the wanted one for which some such product falls at f<sub>IF</sub>. The half-IF spur, an input at f<sub>RF</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub>/2 when the LO is high-side, is the most troublesome because it lies so close to the wanted signal.

sections.h3: Conversion gain and the mixer families

blocks.where: conversion gain as a power ratio; in dB, G<sub>c</sub> = P<sub>IF</sub>(dBm) − P<sub>RF</sub>(dBm). A negative value is conversion loss.

blocks.text: A switch driven by a square LO multiplies the signal by a waveform whose fundamental has amplitude 4/π times that of the square wave's ±1 swing; keeping one of the two output terms leaves a voltage conversion gain of 2/π, that is −3.9 dB, for an ideal double-balanced switching mixer. Real passive mixers (a diode ring or a CMOS switch quad) show 5 to 7 dB of loss. They need a strong LO, typically +7 dBm or more for a diode ring, draw no DC current and have a high IIP3, though they still compress when the RF level nears the LO drive. Their SSB noise figure is close to their loss.

An active mixer adds gain. In the Gilbert cell a differential pair converts the RF voltage into a current (g<sub>m</sub>), two cross-coupled pairs switched by the LO commutate that current, and load resistors R<sub>L</sub> turn it back into voltage. Its voltage conversion gain is (2/π)g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>L</sub>. A single-balanced mixer has one switching pair and lets the LO through to the output; the double-balanced Gilbert cell cancels both the LO and the RF at the IF port, which is why it is the standard choice on chip. Active mixers need less LO power but add more noise and have a lower IIP3.

A mixer converts noise from both the wanted band and the image band to the IF. Its double-sideband (DSB) noise figure assumes the signal is present in both bands, as in a zero-IF receiver; the single-sideband (SSB) figure assumes the signal is in one band only, as in a superheterodyne. Without image filtering, the SSB value is about 3 dB higher than the DSB value.

Isolation is the loss between two ports: LO-to-RF, LO-to-IF and RF-to-IF, in dB. LO-to-RF leakage sends the LO back out to the LNA and antenna; in a zero-IF receiver it self-mixes to a DC offset. LO-to-IF leakage puts a large tone at the IF output that can overload the next stage. These leaks are direct feedthrough at the original frequencies; they are not translated signals and not the image. Balanced circuits and careful layout give 30 to 50 dB of isolation.

examples.question: A down-converter receives RF at 2.45 GHz with a 100 MHz IF and a high-side LO. (a) Find the LO and image frequencies. (b) The mixer is a double-balanced Gilbert cell with g<sub>m</sub> = 20 mS and R<sub>L</sub> = 500 Ω; find its voltage conversion gain. (c) The LO is +7 dBm and the LO-to-RF isolation is 40 dB; find the LO power that leaks back to the RF port.
steps: Image: f<sub>si</sub> = f<sub>LO</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub> = 2.65 GHz (2f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>RF</sub> = 5.10 − 2.45).
g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>L</sub> = 0.02 × 500 = 10; conversion gain = (2/π) × 10 = 6.37, that is 20 log₁₀ 6.37 = 16.1 dB.
Leaked LO at the RF port: 7 − 40 = −33 dBm at 2.55 GHz, which the LNA's reverse isolation must stop before it reaches the antenna.
examples.answer: f<sub>LO</sub> = 2.55 GHz, image 2.65 GHz, conversion gain 6.37 (16.1 dB), LO leakage −33 dBm at the RF port.

examples.question: For the same mixer (f<sub>LO</sub> = 2.55 GHz, f<sub>IF</sub> = 100 MHz), find every RF input between 2.4 and 2.7 GHz for which a product |m·f<sub>LO</sub> − n·f<sub>RF</sub>| with m, n ≤ 3 falls at 100 MHz. Which is the hardest to filter?
steps: Solve m·f<sub>LO</sub> − n·f<sub>RF</sub> = ±0.10 GHz for f<sub>RF</sub> = (m·f<sub>LO</sub> ∓ 0.10)/n.
m = n = 1: f<sub>RF</sub> = 2.55 − 0.10 = 2.45 GHz (wanted) or 2.55 + 0.10 = 2.65 GHz (image).
m = n = 2: f<sub>RF</sub> = (5.10 ∓ 0.10)/2 = 2.50 GHz or 2.60 GHz. Check 2.50: 2 × 2.55 − 2 × 2.50 = 0.10 GHz. This is the half-IF spur, f<sub>RF</sub> + f<sub>IF</sub>/2.
No other m, n ≤ 3 gives an input in 2.4 to 2.7 GHz (for example m = 1, n = 2 gives 1.225 and 1.325 GHz, out of the band).

The 2.50 GHz half-IF spur is only 50 MHz above the wanted 2.45 GHz, half the distance of the image, so the preselector rejects it least. Its strength depends on the mixer's second-order linearity (IIP2), which balanced mixers improve.
examples.answer: Spurs at 2.50, 2.517, 2.583 and 2.60 GHz besides the 2.65 GHz image; the 2.50 GHz half-IF spur, 50 MHz from the signal, is the hardest to filter.

traps: Using f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>RF</sub> − f<sub>IF</sub> for a high-side LO, which gives the wrong LO and the wrong image.
Forgetting that a switching mixer also responds to m·f<sub>LO</sub> ± n·f<sub>RF</sub>; the image is only the m = n = 1 spur.
Writing conversion loss as a positive gain: a mixer with 6 dB loss turns −20 dBm into −26 dBm, so G<sub>c</sub> = −6 dB.
Confusing isolation with image rejection. LO leakage appears at f<sub>LO</sub>; the image is a different input frequency that converts to f<sub>IF</sub>.
Quoting the DSB noise figure for a superheterodyne, where the signal is in one sideband only and the SSB figure (about 3 dB higher) applies.

quiz.q: Name the three ports of a mixer and the signal at each.
quiz.a: RF port: the radio-frequency signal; LO port: the local-oscillator drive; IF port: the frequency-shifted output.

quiz.q: Why does a passive switching mixer have conversion loss?
quiz.a: It has no gain element; switching splits the signal between the sum and difference products and the harmonics, and only one product is kept. The ideal limit is 2/π (−3.9 dB); switch resistance adds more.

quiz.q: A down-converter has RF = 900 MHz, IF = 45 MHz and a high-side LO. Find the LO, the image and the half-IF spur.
A mixer has conversion gain +8 dB. Find the IF output for −30 dBm at the RF port, and for the same input through a passive mixer with 6 dB loss.
Why is a double-balanced mixer preferred to a single-balanced one?
quiz.a: Its symmetry cancels both the LO and the RF signal at the IF port, giving better LO-to-IF and RF-to-IF isolation and suppressing even-order spurs.

quiz.q: Why is the SSB noise figure of a mixer about 3 dB above its DSB noise figure?
quiz.a: Noise from both the signal band and the image band is converted to the IF. If the signal is present in both bands (DSB) the two noise contributions are matched by two signal contributions; with signal in one band only (SSB) the same noise meets half the signal, so the SNR is 3 dB worse.

quiz.q: In a zero-IF receiver, what does LO-to-RF leakage cause?
quiz.a: The leaked LO reaches the RF port, passes into the mixer with the signal and mixes with the LO itself, giving a DC offset at baseband that can saturate the baseband amplifiers; if it reaches the antenna it is also radiated.

beyond: Not for the exam. Many modern receivers use passive CMOS mixers driven by 25 % duty-cycle LO pulses, which improve gain and noise over the 50 % case, and mixer-first receivers place the switches straight at the antenna. Harmonic-reject mixers combine several phases of the LO to cancel the 3f<sub>LO</sub> and 5f<sub>LO</sub> responses in wideband TV and software radios. Search for '25% duty cycle passive mixer', 'harmonic reject mixer' and 'mixer spur chart'.
